lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Living things are classified into groups on the basis of similar characteristics.
  • Birds that live in water, like the duck, have webbed feet to help them swim, while land birds like the hen have separate toes with claws.
  • The cat is a mammal; mammals give birth to their young ones and feed them on milk.
  • A fish respires through gills.
  • Seeds with one cotyledon are monocots (wheat, rice, maize) and seeds with two cotyledons are dicots (pea, bean, gram).
  • Monocot leaves have parallel veins and dicot leaves have net-like veins.
  • Echinoderms are the group found only in the ocean.

Solved Exercises

Q: Which one of the following is the foot of an aquatic bird? (Options are pictures labelled A, B, C and D)

Options: (a) A — webbed foot (b) B — foot with thick separate toes and claws (c) C — foot with thin separate toes and claws (d) D — foot with thin separate toes and claws

Correct answer: A — webbed foot

Q: The cat belongs to which group?

Options: (a) Amphibians (b) Reptiles (c) Birds (d) Mammals

Correct answer: Mammals

Q: A fish respires through which organ?

Options: (a) Gills (b) Lungs (c) Air sacs (d) Skin

Correct answer: Gills

Q: What is the number of cotyledons in a gram seed?

Options: (a) One (b) Two (c) Three (d) Four

Correct answer: Two

Q: Out of these which group is found only in ocean?

Options: (a) Fish (b) Insects (c) Echinoderms (d) Amphibians

Correct answer: Echinoderms

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is the foot of an aquatic bird?
options: Foot with thick separate toes and claws
Foot with thin separate toes and claws
Foot with thin toes and no claws
mcqs.why: An aquatic bird such as the duck lives in water, so it has a webbed foot which helps it to swim, as stated in the chapter.

mcqs.q: The cat belongs to which group?
mcqs.why: The cat belongs to mammals. In the grouping activity the cat is placed with goat, tiger and cow in the mammals group.

mcqs.q: A fish respires through which organ?
mcqs.why: A fish respires through gills. Gills are the respiratory organ of fish given in the book's keyed answer for this question.

mcqs.q: What is the number of cotyledons in a gram seed?
mcqs.why: A gram seed has two cotyledons, so gram is a dicot plant. Pea, bean and gram are the dicot examples in Activity 1.2.

mcqs.q: Out of these which group is found only in ocean?
mcqs.why: Echinoderms are found only in the ocean. This is the book's keyed answer; fish, insects and amphibians are not limited to the ocean.

mcqs.q: Which of the following seeds has only one cotyledon?
mcqs.why: Wheat has one cotyledon and is a monocot plant, along with rice and maize. Pea, bean and gram have two cotyledons.

mcqs.q: What is the arrangement of veins in the leaves of a monocot plant?
options: Veins in the form of a net
mcqs.why: In a monocot leaf the veins are parallel to each other. Dicot leaves, by contrast, have veins in the form of a net.

mcqs.q: A pigeon is a vertebrate because it has:
options: An internal skeleton made of bones
mcqs.why: The pigeon has an internal skeleton made of bones, so it is a vertebrate. Its body is covered with feathers and it has a beak.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a flowering plant?
mcqs.why: Rose is a flowering plant, grouped with guava, mango and sunflower. Fowl, pigeon and sparrow are birds, not plants.

mcqs.q: How many floral leaves does a monocot flower usually have?
options: Three or a multiple of three
mcqs.why: A monocot flower has three floral leaves or a multiple of three. A dicot flower usually has four or five floral leaves or their multiple.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Biodiversity is the number of kinds of living things present at a particular place.
  • Classification helps us determine similarities and differences among organisms, identify and study them, and know their relationships.
  • Worms are soft-bodied with no legs, while insects have six jointed legs, a body in head, thorax and abdomen, and a hard exoskeleton.
  • Amphibians live on land and in water, respire through lungs and skin, and lay eggs in water; reptiles have thick, coarse, dry skin and lay eggs on land.
  • Fungi and animals are similar because both lack chlorophyll and cannot make their own food.
  • Monera are one-celled with a very simple structure, e.g. bacteria; Protista usually live in water, e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium and Algae.
  • Cartilage is softer, lighter and more flexible than bone, so sharks and sting rays can swim fast and bend easily in water.

Solved Exercises

Q: Define biodiversity.

Ans: The number of kinds of living things present at a particular place is called biodiversity.

Q: State the importance of classification.

Ans: Due to classification we can determine the similarities and differences among organisms. Due to the structure and other characteristics of organisms we can identify and study them. We can also know the relationship among organisms.

Q: Write the differences between: (a) Worms and Insects

Ans: Worms are soft bodied animals. Their body is round and cylindrical and they have no legs. The body of some worms is segmented, e.g., earthworms, and the body of some worms is not segmented, e.g., flatworms and roundworms. Insects are invertebrates with jointed legs. Their body is segmented and divided into three parts: head, thorax and abdomen. The number of legs is six or three pairs, and the external surface of the body is hard, which is called exoskeleton.

Q: Write the differences between: (b) Amphibians and Reptiles

Ans: Amphibians can live on land and also in water. They respire through lungs and skin, their skin is usually moist and loose, they live on land but lay eggs in water, and their development takes place in water. Reptiles are called creeping animals. Their skin is thick, coarse and dry, which protects their body from external effects, and these animals lay eggs on land. The body temperature of both groups depends on the temperature of their surroundings.

Q: What is the similarity between Fungi and Animals?

Ans: Both fungi and animals do not have chlorophyll, so they cannot make their own food. Fungi absorb food from the place where they live, and animals also obtain their food from other organisms instead of making it themselves.

Q: Write one characteristic and one example of Monera and Protista.

Ans: Monera: These are made of one cell and their structure is also very simple. Example: bacteria. Protista: Usually they live in water and are found in rivers, ponds and ocean. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium and Algae, e.g., Spirogyra.

Q: Some animals have internal skeleton of cartilage such as Shark and Sting Ray. They feed on other animals by predation. What is the importance of cartilage in their life?

Ans: Cartilage is softer, lighter and more flexible than bone. A skeleton of cartilage makes the body of the shark and sting ray light and flexible, so they can swim fast and bend their body easily in water. This helps these animals to move quickly, catch other animals by predation and escape from danger.

mcqs.q: What is biodiversity?
options: The number of kinds of living things at a particular place
The study of rocks at a place
The number of plants in a garden only
The process of making food by plants
mcqs.why: Biodiversity is defined in the chapter as the number of kinds of living things present at a particular place.

mcqs.q: Why is classification important?
options: It changes the characteristics of organisms
It helps us find similarities, differences and relationships among organisms
It helps organisms make their own food
mcqs.why: Due to classification we can determine similarities and differences among organisms, identify and study them, and know the relationship among organisms.

mcqs.q: Which statement about worms is correct?
options: Worms are soft-bodied, round and cylindrical, with no legs
Worms are divided into head, thorax and abdomen
mcqs.why: Worms are soft-bodied animals. Their body is round and cylindrical and they have no legs, unlike insects which have jointed legs.

mcqs.q: How many legs does an insect have?
mcqs.why: Insects have six legs, that is three pairs of jointed legs. Their segmented body is divided into head, thorax and abdomen.

mcqs.q: Where do amphibians lay their eggs?
mcqs.why: Amphibians live on land but lay eggs in water, and their development takes place in water. Reptiles, in contrast, lay eggs on land.

mcqs.q: What kind of skin do reptiles have?
mcqs.why: Reptiles have thick, coarse and dry skin which protects their body from external effects. Amphibians usually have moist and loose skin.

mcqs.q: What is the similarity between fungi and animals?
options: Both can make their own food
Both do not have chlorophyll and cannot make their own food
mcqs.why: Both fungi and animals do not have chlorophyll, so they cannot make their own food. Fungi absorb food and animals obtain food from other organisms.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of Monera?
mcqs.why: Bacteria are the example of Monera given in the chapter. Monera are made of one cell and their structure is very simple.

mcqs.q: Where do Protista usually live?
options: In water, in rivers, ponds and ocean
mcqs.why: Protista usually live in water and are found in rivers, ponds and ocean. Examples are Amoeba, Paramecium and Algae such as Spirogyra.

mcqs.q: Why is a cartilage skeleton useful for a shark?
options: It makes the body heavy and hard
It helps the shark live on land
It is softer, lighter and more flexible than bone, so the shark can swim fast and bend easily
It helps the shark make its own food
mcqs.why: Cartilage is softer, lighter and more flexible than bone. It makes the shark's body light and flexible so it can swim fast, bend easily, catch prey and escape danger.

lessons.title: Investigate and Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Investigate and Project Work

Q: Why the body of zebra has black and white stripes?

Ans: The black and white stripes on the body of the zebra help it to hide in its surroundings and confuse the animals that hunt it. When zebras stand together in a group, the stripes make it difficult for a hunter animal to single out one zebra, so the stripes protect the zebra.

Q: Why are the ears of elephant large?

Ans: The elephant lives in a hot climate. Its large ears help it to lose extra heat from its body and keep the body cool. The elephant also uses its large ears to hear sounds from far away.

Q: Investigate about the factors responsible for the extinction of biodiversity.

Ans: The main factors are human actions. The forests are being cut for cultivation and urbanization (extension of cities), which has destroyed the habitats of animals. Secondly, the human act of excessive hunting has made animals endangered. When habitats are destroyed and hunting continues, organisms decrease in number and finally become extinct, e.g., dinosaurs have become extinct.

Q: Give an example of extinct and endangered animals. Investigate what types of animals are most likely to be extinct?

Ans: Extinct animals: dinosaurs, which are no longer found in this world. Endangered animals: Bengal tiger, Panda, snow leopard, green turtle, hawk, Indus dolphin and markhor. The animals most likely to become extinct are the endangered organisms, i.e., those organisms that are very likely to become extinct in the near future because their number has become very small.

Q: Project: Album of Animals. Required Materials: Old newspaper and magzines, Scissors, Gum, Coloured markers, Album. Procedure: Cut pictures of two animals from each of the five groups of vertebrates. The pictures can also be obtained from internet. Paste the pictures on album. Write characteristics of each animal with its picture.

Ans: The completed album will contain ten pictures, two animals from each of the five groups of vertebrates — fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals — with the characteristics of each animal written with its picture. Example (fish, as printed in the book): It has fins and tails. Its body has scales. Its body is boat-shaped. In the same way, the characteristics of the animals of the other four groups are written from the chapter, e.g., amphibians live on land and in water, reptiles have thick, coarse and dry skin, birds have feathers and beak, and mammals give birth to their young ones and feed them on milk.

lessons.title: Activities and Points to Ponder
lessons.notes_html:
Activities and Points to Ponder

Activity 1.1

Q: Write the names of the following organism in their respective groups on the basis of similar characteristics. Guava, fowl, pigeon, mango, sparrow, snake, rose, crocodile, sunflower, lizard, cat, tiger, cow, tortoise, goat, dove.

Ans: Group 1 (flowering plants): Rose, guava, mango, sunflower. Group 2 (birds): Fowl, pigeon, sparrow, dove. Group 3 (reptiles): Snake, crocodile, lizard, tortoise. Group 4 (mammals): Goat, cat, tiger, cow. Each group is made of organisms that have similar characteristics.

Q: Why did you put rose in one group and fowl in another group?

Ans: Rose and fowl were put in separate groups because they have different characteristics. Rose is a flowering plant, while fowl is a bird. Organisms of similar characteristics are placed in one group, so the rose was grouped with the other flowering plants (mango, guava and sunflower) and the fowl was grouped with the other birds (pigeon, dove and sparrow).

Point to Ponder!

Q: What is the difference between the paws of hen and duck?

Ans: The duck lives in water, so it has webbed feet which help it to swim. The hen lives on land, so its feet have separate toes with claws and are not webbed. The chapter states that the birds that live in water have webbed feet, e.g., duck.

Activity 1.2

Q: Take the seeds of wheat, rice, maize, pea, bean and gram. Find out in which seed there is one cotyledon and in which seed there are two cotyledons. Write your observations.

Ans: Seeds with one cotyledon (monocot plants): wheat, rice and maize. Seeds with two cotyledons (dicot plants): pea, bean and gram. The flowering plants whose seeds have one cotyledon are called monocot plants, and the flowering plants whose seeds have two cotyledons are called dicot plants.

Activity 1.3

Q: Observe the leaves of monocot and dicot plants. What is the arrangement of veins in these leaves?

Ans: In the leaves of a monocot plant, the veins are parallel to each other. The leaves of dicot plants have veins in the form of a net.

Q: Take flowers of monocot and dicot plants and count the number of floral leaves.

Ans: The small leaves of a flower are called floral leaves. The number of floral leaves in a flower of monocot plant is three or multiple of three. The number of floral leaves in a flower of dicot plant is usually four or five or their multiple.

Activity 1.5

Q: Look at the pictures of pigeon and butterfly. What differences do you see between the two? Write your observations.

Ans: The pigeon is a vertebrate. It has an internal skeleton made of bones, and its body is covered with feathers. It has a beak and can fly. The butterfly is an invertebrate. It has no bone inside its body. It is an insect, so its body is segmented and divided into head, thorax and abdomen, it has six jointed legs, and the external surface of its body is hard, which is called exoskeleton.

Point to Ponder!

Q: What is the difference between a toad and a frog?

Ans: Frog and toad are both amphibians, so both can live on land and in water, respire through lungs and skin, lay eggs in water and their body temperature depends on the temperature of their surroundings. The frog has smooth and moist skin and lives nearer to water, while the toad has rough and dry skin.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Microorganisms include viruses, bacteria, fungi and protozoa; an ant is not a microorganism.
  • Mushrooms and Penicillium both belong to the fungi group of microorganisms.
  • Polio is caused by a virus.
  • Food becomes contaminated because of microorganisms present in the environment.
  • Viruses are not fully living: they reproduce only inside a living body and are nonliving outside it.
  • Bacteria are found in every type of environment — in air, water, soil and inside living things.
  • Yeast is a fungus that uses sugar as food and releases carbon dioxide gas, which makes dough rise and become soft.

Solved Exercises

Q: Mushrooms belong to which group of microorganisms?

Options: (a) Virus (b) Fungi (c) Bacteria (d) Protozoa

Correct answer: Fungi

Q: What is the cause of the polio disease?

Options: (a) Protozoa (b) Virus (c) Fungi (d) Bacteria

Correct answer: Virus

Q: Penicillium is an example of which group?

Options: (a) Protozoa (b) Fungi (c) Bacteria (d) Virus

Correct answer: Fungi

Q: The food is contaminated due to the presence of __________ in the environment.

Options: (a) moisture (b) microorganisms (c) air (d) heat

Correct answer: microorganisms

Q: Which one of the following is not a microorganism?

Options: (a) Bacteria (b) Virus (c) Protozoa (d) Ant

Correct answer: Ant

mcqs.q: Mushrooms belong to which group of microorganisms?
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is fungi. Mushrooms are large fungi, so they belong to the fungi group of microorganisms, not to viruses, bacteria or protozoa.

mcqs.q: What is the cause of the polio disease?
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is virus. Polio is caused by a virus, which reproduces only inside the living body of its host.

mcqs.q: Penicillium is an example of which group?
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is fungi. Penicillium is a fungus, and fungi and bacteria are also used to make antibiotics such as those from Penicillium.

mcqs.q: The food is contaminated due to the presence of __________ in the environment.
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is microorganisms. Pathogens present in contaminated food enter the human body when the food is eaten and cause diseases such as diarrhoea.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is not a microorganism?
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is ant. Bacteria, viruses and protozoa are all microorganisms, but an ant is a small insect that can be seen easily, so it is not a microorganism.

mcqs.q: Viruses can reproduce only when they are:
mcqs.why: The chapter states that viruses can reproduce only within an organism. Outside the body of an organism they are nonliving, so they behave as living things only inside a living body.

mcqs.q: In which places are bacteria found?
options: In air, water, soil and inside living things
mcqs.why: The chapter states that bacteria are found in every type of environment. They are found in air, water, soil and inside living things, not in just one of these places.

mcqs.q: Which gas released by yeast makes dough rise and become soft?
mcqs.why: Yeast is a fungus that uses sugar as its food and releases carbon dioxide gas. This gas is produced inside the dough, so the dough rises and becomes soft.

mcqs.q: How do germs spread when a sick person coughs or sneezes?
options: They travel only through drinking water
They spread into the air and are breathed in by a healthy person
They spread only by shaking hands
They cannot spread to another person
mcqs.why: In Activity 2.3 the paper pieces scattered out of the balloon just as germs spread on coughing or sneezing. When a healthy person breathes in this air, the pathogens enter his body and he becomes sick.

mcqs.q: What do decomposers do to dead plants and animals?
options: They turn them into living plants again
They hide them under the soil forever
They break them down into simple components
mcqs.why: Decomposers break down dead organisms into their simple components so these become part of the ecosystem again. Without decomposers, dead bodies would keep piling up and matter would not be recycled.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pathogens are microorganisms that cause diseases in their hosts; the diseases they cause are called infections or infectious diseases.
  • Pathogens enter the body in five main ways: through air, water, food, animals and direct contact.
  • Some bacteria and fungi are called decomposers because they break the organic molecules of food and dead bodies into simple components.
  • Bacteria are useful: they help in digestion in the small intestine and are used in making yoghurt.
  • Bacteria are also harmful: they cause diseases such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, diarrhoea, typhoid and cholera, and they spoil food such as milk.
  • A mosquito transmits malaria and dengue by taking pathogens from a patient's blood and passing them to a healthy person when it bites.
  • Decomposition happens faster where it is hot and moist, because its rate increases with temperature, humidity and oxygen.

Solved Exercises

Q: What is a pathogen? How does it enter in the bodies of organisms?

Ans: The microorganisms that cause diseases in their hosts are called pathogens, and the diseases that occur due to them are called infections or infectious diseases. Pathogens enter the bodies of organisms through five main ways: air, water, food, animals and direct contact. For example, they are breathed in with air, taken in with polluted water or contaminated food, transmitted by animals such as mosquitoes, or passed on by shaking hands or touching articles used by a patient.

Q: Why are some bacteria and fungi called decomposers?

Ans: Some bacteria and fungi are called decomposers because during decomposition they break the organic molecules of food and dead bodies into simple components. The organisms which do decomposition are called decomposers.

Q: Write two benefits and two harmful effects of bacteria.

Ans: Benefits of bacteria: (1) Some bacteria help in the digestion of food and absorption of food components in our small intestine. (2) Bacteria are used in making yoghurt, and as decomposers they break down dead bodies and can also be used to decompose toxic materials present in sewerage and industrial waste water. Harmful effects of bacteria: (1) They cause diseases in plants, animals and humans, e.g., pneumonia, tuberculosis, diarrhea, typhoid and cholera. (2) By decomposition they damage and spoil food, e.g., milk is spoiled because of them.

Q: How does the microorganism yeast work to soften and rise dough of flour?

Ans: Yeast is a fungus used in making bread. When yeast is mixed in flour along with sugar and water, it uses the sugar as food and releases carbon dioxide gas. This gas is produced inside the dough, so the dough rises and becomes soft, as observed in Activity 2.4, where the dough with yeast and sugar rose in one hour while the dough without yeast did not rise.

Q: How does a mosquito transmit disease?

Ans: Some animals transmit pathogens from one human to the others. When a mosquito bites and sucks blood of a patient of malaria or dengue, it takes pathogens from the patient. When it bites a healthy person, it transmits those pathogens into him, and the healthy person becomes sick.

Q: The soil of forests of hot climate is always hot and moist, whereas the soil of forests of cold climate is cold and dry. Out of these two areas where the decomposition of fallen leaves will happen more quickly? Explain.

Ans: Decomposition of fallen leaves will happen more quickly in the forest of hot climate. The rate of decomposition increases with increase in temperature, humidity and oxygen. The soil of the hot climate forest is hot and moist, which gives the bacteria and fungi the warmth and humidity they need to work faster, while the cold and dry soil of the cold climate forest slows decomposition down.

mcqs.q: What is a pathogen?
options: A microorganism that causes disease in its host
A small insect that bites people
mcqs.why: The chapter defines pathogens as the microorganisms that cause diseases in their hosts, and the diseases that occur due to them are called infections or infectious diseases.

mcqs.q: Pathogens enter the bodies of organisms through which ways?
options: Through air, water, food, animals and direct contact
Only through direct contact with a patient
mcqs.why: The chapter lists five main ways pathogens enter the body: air, water, food, animals and direct contact, such as breathing them in, drinking polluted water, or shaking hands with a patient.

mcqs.q: Why are some bacteria and fungi called decomposers?
options: Because they break organic molecules of food and dead bodies into simple components
Because they cause polio and malaria
Because they live only inside living things
mcqs.why: Some bacteria and fungi are called decomposers because during decomposition they break the organic molecules of food and dead bodies into simple components.

mcqs.q: How do some bacteria help us inside our own body?
options: They help in the digestion and absorption of food in the small intestine
They protect our skin from sunlight
mcqs.why: One benefit of bacteria given in the chapter is that some bacteria help in the digestion of food and absorption of food components in our small intestine.

mcqs.q: Bacteria are used in making which food item?
mcqs.why: The chapter states that bacteria are used in making yoghurt. Yeast, not bacteria, is the microorganism used in making bread.

mcqs.q: Which of these diseases is caused by bacteria?
mcqs.why: The chapter lists pneumonia, tuberculosis, diarrhoea, typhoid and cholera as diseases caused by bacteria. Polio is caused by a virus, while malaria and dengue pathogens are carried by mosquitoes.

mcqs.q: When yeast is mixed in flour, what does it use as its food?
mcqs.why: When yeast is mixed in flour along with sugar and water, it uses the sugar as food and releases carbon dioxide gas, which makes the dough rise and become soft.

mcqs.q: How does a mosquito transmit malaria or dengue to a healthy person?
options: It lays eggs in the person's food
It takes pathogens from a patient's blood and passes them on when it bites a healthy person
It spreads pathogens through the air when it flies
It touches the person's skin with its wings
mcqs.why: When a mosquito bites and sucks the blood of a patient of malaria or dengue, it takes pathogens from the patient, and when it bites a healthy person it transmits those pathogens into him.

mcqs.q: In which forest will fallen leaves decompose more quickly?
options: In a forest with cold and dry soil
In a forest with no oxygen
In a forest with hot and moist soil
mcqs.why: The rate of decomposition increases with increase in temperature, humidity and oxygen. Hot and moist soil gives bacteria and fungi the warmth and humidity they need to work faster, while cold and dry soil slows decomposition down.

mcqs.q: Why does using too much antibacterial soap increase the chance of infection?
options: The soap makes harmful bacteria stronger
The soap removes the useful bacteria on the skin that protect us
The soap attracts mosquitoes to the skin
The soap stops us from washing with water
mcqs.why: Antibacterial soap also kills the useful bacteria living on our skin that protect us. When excessive use of soap removes these useful bacteria, the skin loses its protection and harmful bacteria get a better chance to grow and cause infection.

lessons.title: Investigate and Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Investigate and Project Work

Q: “All microorganism are harmful and cause diseases”. Prove that this idea is incorrect.

Ans: This idea is incorrect because all microorganisms are not harmful. Many microorganisms are useful in everyday life: bacteria and yeasts are used in making food items — yeasts are used to make bread and cheese and bacteria are used in making yoghurt; many microorganisms are used for making medicines, and fungi and bacteria are used to make antibiotics; and bacteria clean the environment by decomposing dead bodies and toxic materials in sewerage and industrial waste water. Only some microorganisms are pathogens that cause diseases.

Q: Many people use antibacterial soap to kill the bacteria present on their hands. But due to excessive use of soap, the chance of getting infection increases instead of descreasing. Why does it happen?

Ans: Antibacterial soap kills the bacteria present on the hands, including the useful bacteria. The number of harmful bacteria is very less and a large number of bacteria are useful for humans, and the normal bacteria living on our skin protect us. When excessive use of soap removes these useful bacteria as well, the skin loses its protection, so harmful bacteria get a better chance to grow and cause infection. That is why the chance of getting infection increases instead of decreasing.

Q: Project: The effect of quantity of sugar on the release of carbon dioxide from yeast. Requirements: Teaspoon, Rubber band, Balloons, Transparent bottles of one litre (4 number), Marker, Yeast, Sugar, Warm water. Procedure: Take four transparent plastic bottles and label them as I, II, III and IV. Add a teaspoon of yeast in each bottle. Add sugar in each bottle as per given table (Bottle I: 0 teaspoons, Bottle II: 1 teaspoon, Bottle III: 2 teaspoons, Bottle IV: 3 teaspoons). Do not add sugar in the first bottle. Pour half cup of hot water in each bottle. Immediately, put a balloon at the mouth of each bottle and bind it strongly with rubber band. Shake each bottle strongly so that its contents can mix up. Leave all the bottles in this condition for twenty minutes. Then observe:

Ans: The balloons inflate because the yeast in each bottle uses the sugar and releases carbon dioxide gas, which fills the balloon. The balloon on bottle IV, which has the most sugar (3 teaspoons), inflates the most; the balloon on bottle III (2 teaspoons) inflates less, the balloon on bottle II (1 teaspoon) inflates still less, and the balloon on bottle I (no sugar) does not inflate, as shown in the figure. This shows that the greater the quantity of sugar, the more carbon dioxide is released by the yeast.

Q: Which balloon inflated the most?

Ans: The balloon on bottle IV inflated the most, because bottle IV contained the greatest quantity of sugar (3 teaspoons).

Q: In which bottle, most carbon dioxide gas was produced?

Ans: Most carbon dioxide gas was produced in bottle IV, which had 3 teaspoons of sugar, the greatest quantity of sugar. The balloon on this bottle inflated the most, which shows that most gas was produced in it.

lessons.title: Points to Ponder and Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Points to Ponder and Activities

Point to ponder!

Q: Do you think that viruses are living organisms. Why?

Ans: Viruses are not fully living organisms. They are the link between living and nonliving things. They can reproduce only within an organism, and out of the body of an organism they are nonliving. So a virus behaves as a living thing only inside a living body and as a nonliving thing outside it.

Q: In what types of environment bacteria live?

Ans: Bacteria are found in every type of environment. They are found in air, water, soil and inside living things.

Point to Ponder!

Q: What if there were no decomposers in the world?

Ans: If decomposers do not exist, then it is impossible to break down dead organisms into their simple components to make these a part of the ecosystem. Dead bodies of plants and animals would keep piling up, carbon dioxide and nitrogen gases would not be released back into the environment, and the producers would not get simple materials again to make their food, so matter would not be recycled.

Activity 2.2

Q: When a boy came home from school, he felt hunger. He saw raw chicken in the kitchen. He took a piece of chicken, put pepper and salt on it, cooked and ate it while watching TV. At midnight the boy got up due to diarrhea, fever and stomach pain. In his school, there was an epidemic of diarrhea. So, his mother met the principal of the school. She asked the principal about what did the boy eat during the break? The principal informed her that he would find out whether the boy fell ill due to eating something in the school or not. In your opinion why did the boy fell ill?

Ans: The boy most likely fell ill because of the chicken he cooked and ate at home. The chapter explains that pathogens of some diseases are present in contaminated food, and on eating such food these pathogens enter the human body and cause diseases such as diarrhea. His diarrhea, fever and stomach pain started at midnight, after eating the chicken at home, so the cause was the contaminated or improperly cooked food eaten at home and not necessarily anything eaten in the school.

Ans: The pieces of paper scattered out of the balloon. In the same way, the germs are spread on coughing or sneezing, and when a healthy person breathes in this air, these pathogens enter his body and he becomes sick.

Ans: The dough has risen in the first pot, in which yeast and sugar were mixed, while the dough in the second pot, in which only sugar was mixed, did not rise. The reason is that yeast is a microorganism (fungus) which uses sugar as its food and releases carbon dioxide gas, and this gas makes the dough rise and become soft. Sugar was added along with yeast to provide food to the yeast, so that it could work and produce the gas.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A flower has four parts: sepals protect the internal structures, and petals attract insects and birds towards the flower.
  • The stamen is the male part, made of the anther, where pollen grains are formed, and the filament, which supports the anther.
  • The carpel is the female part: pollen grains adhere and germinate on the stigma, the pollen tube passes through the style, and the ovary contains one or more ovules.
  • In self pollination pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower or the same plant, as in pea, cotton and tomato; in cross pollination it reaches a flower of another plant of the same type, as in maize, papaya and rose.
  • Reproduction is the process by which living things produce new organisms of their own kind so that their generation continues.
  • In germination the seed absorbs water through its micropyle, swells and the seed coat bursts; the radicle grows down into roots and the plumule grows up into a shoot.
  • If all insects became extinct, insect-pollinated flowers would produce no seeds or fruits, and their number would decrease greatly.

Solved Exercises

Q: Can you tell the names and functions of the four parts of a flower?

Ans: The four parts of a flower are: (1) Sepals — green leaflets that form the first whorl; they protect the internal structures. (2) Petals — coloured leaflets that form the second whorl; they attract insects and birds towards the flower. (3) Stamen — the third whorl and the male reproductive part; it consists of the anther, where pollen grains are formed, and the filament, which supports the anther. (4) Carpel — the fourth whorl and the female reproductive part; it consists of the stigma, on which pollen grains adhere and germinate, the style, through which the pollen tube passes, and the ovary, which has one or more ovules.

Q: How will you compare self pollination and cross pollination?

Ans: In self pollination, pollen grains are transferred from the anther of a flower to the stigma of the same flower, or to the stigma of another flower of the same plant; it takes place in pea, cotton and tomato. In cross pollination, pollen grains are transferred from the flower of one plant to the stigma of the flower of another plant of the same type; it takes place in maize, papaya and rose.

Q: Compare gram and maize seed?

Ans: Gram seed has two cotyledons, while maize seed has one cotyledon, so maize is a monocot plant. In gram seed the endosperm is absent and food is stored in the cotyledons, while in maize seed the endosperm is present and food is stored in it. In gram seed the embryo is present at the centre of the seed, while in maize seed the embryo is present at one side of the seed. Gram seed is conical, pear-shaped and light brown with a thick seed coat, while maize seed is oval and flat with a thin seed coat.

Q: Define reproduction.

Ans: Reproduction is the process by which living things produce new organisms of their own kind, so that their generation continues. The life span of living things is limited and sooner or later they die, but through reproduction life continues on the Earth. In plants, reproduction is of two types: asexual reproduction, in which only one parent produces new plants, and sexual reproduction, which takes place through flowers.

Q: Label the given picture.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The picture is a longitudinal section of a flower on its stalk, the pedicel, at the bottom. At the base of the flower are the green leaf-like sepals. Above them are the large coloured petals. In the centre stands the carpel (female part): its top is the stigma, on which pollen grains are sitting, below it is the narrow neck-like style, and at its base is the swollen ovary, which contains the ovules inside it. Around the carpel stand the stamens (male parts), each made of a long stalk, the filament, topped by an oval anther, in which pollen grains are formed.

Q: Observe the given picture. What is the role of water in seed germination?

Ans: Water is necessary for seed germination. During germination the seed absorbs water through its micropyle. On absorbing water, the seed swells and the seed coat bursts. The cotyledons then provide food to the radicle and plumule; the radicle grows towards the ground and gives rise to roots, and the plumule grows upwards and gives rise to a tiny shoot. Without water the seed does not germinate, as shown in the germination experiment in the chapter, where seeds on dry cotton did not germinate while seeds on wet cotton did.

Q: Observe the given pictures. For which type of pollination, the shapes and structures of flowers are suitable?

Ans: The pictures show a butterfly, a bird and bees visiting flowers. Such flowers are suitable for cross pollination through insects and birds (animals). The chapter states that petals attract insects and birds towards the flower and that most of the pollination takes place through insects and air (pollination also takes place through bats and water). When these animals visit a flower, pollen grains stick to their bodies and are carried to the stigma of a flower of another plant of the same type, which is cross pollination.

Q: If all the insects become extinct, what will be its effect on flowering plants?

Ans: Most of the pollination takes place through insects (and air), and the petals of flowers attract insects for this purpose. If all insects become extinct, the flowers that depend on insects for pollination will not be pollinated. Without pollination there will be no fertilisation, so such plants will produce no seeds and no fruits, and their number will decrease greatly. Only the plants pollinated by wind, water or bats would continue to reproduce in the normal way.

The parts also differ from flower to flower: sepals are green leaflets, petals differ in colour, size and number, stamens differ in number, and the carpel may be single or, as in China rose, there may be more than one carpel in a flower.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Causes of air pollution: poisonous substances in smoke from vehicles, smoke from factories, burning of fuels in kilns and homes, and forest fires.
  • Effects of pollution: germs in polluted water cause diseases, bacteria in sewerage use dissolved oxygen so fish die, smog causes lung diseases and allergy, and acid rain harms buildings, trees and aquatic life.
  • Greenhouse effect: carbon dioxide and other gases allow sunlight to reach the Earth but do not allow the heat of the Earth to leave, so the Earth remains hot.
  • Global warming: burning fossil fuel increases greenhouse gases and the Earth's temperature; melting ice at the poles raises sea level, causing more rains and floods, and coastal areas and islands may disappear.
  • Preventive measures: shift factories away from cities, do not pour polluted water into rivers, canals and lakes, dispose of garbage properly, reduce and ban smoke-emitting vehicles, reduce cutting of trees and plant more trees.
  • Biodegradable materials break down into simple substances and become part of the soil, e.g. vegetable and fruit peels, meat, bread, rice and paper; non-biodegradable materials like polythene bags, plastic bottles and computer components do not break down.
  • The 4R principle to reduce non-biodegradable materials is: recycle, reuse, reduce and refuse.

Solved Exercises

Q: Write three causes of air pollution.

Ans: Three causes of air pollution given in the chapter are: (1) the poisonous substances present in the smoke emitted from vehicles; (2) the smoke emitted from factories; and (3) the burning of fuels in kilns and homes, which produces carbon dioxide gas. Forest fires are another cause of air pollution.

Q: What are the four effects of pollution on life?

Ans: Four effects of pollution on life are: (1) germs present in polluted water cause diseases; (2) bacteria present in sewerage use most of the dissolved oxygen in water, so aquatic animals such as fish die due to lack of oxygen; (3) pollutants such as chemicals, carbon dioxide and other gases in polluted air cause throat, skin and eye diseases, and pollutant gases in smog cause lung diseases and allergy; and (4) poisonous substances from factory chimneys dissolve in rain water and produce acid rain, which harms buildings and trees and also the aquatic life of streams, canals and lakes.

Q: What is greenhouse effect?

Ans: Carbon dioxide and other gases present in our environment work like the glass of a greenhouse. They allow the sunlight to reach the Earth, but they do not allow the heat of the Earth to leave. This process is called the greenhouse effect. Due to this, our Earth remains hot.

Q: What will be the effects of Global warming?

Ans: When fossil fuel is burnt, carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases increase, which results in an increase in the temperature of the Earth; this is called global warming. Due to global warming the climate of the world is changing. The melting of ice from the North and South poles is increasing the level of sea water, which is causing more rains and floods. If this process continues, the coastal areas and islands may disappear in the sea.

Q: Write three ways of preventive measures to reduce pollution.

Ans: Three preventive measures to reduce pollution are: (1) factories should be shifted away from the cities, and the smoke of factories should be made ineffective before releasing it in the air; (2) polluted water should not be poured into rivers, canals and lakes, and the garbage and solid wastes of houses should be disposed of in a proper way; and (3) the number of vehicles should be reduced and smoke-emitting vehicles should be banned. Cutting of trees should also be reduced and there should be more tree plantation.

Q: What is the main cause of pollution?

Ans: Pollution is caused by the pollutants — the harmful substances that are added to the environment by human activities. The chapter gives these main causes: smoke emitted by vehicles and factories, burning of fuels in kilns and homes, sewerage and factory wastes thrown into water, oil leakages from oil tankers, insecticides and fertilizers, and garbage scattered on land with no proper arrangement for its disposal. Any such change in the environment which is harmful for living things is environmental pollution.

Q: Why Government of Pakistan has banned the use of polythene bags?

Ans: Polythene bags are a non-biodegradable material: they cannot break down into simple substances by natural processes. Thrown-away polythene bags therefore remain in the environment for a long time and keep causing land pollution (and also pollute water), so the Government of Pakistan has banned the use of polythene bags.

Q: If it is written D2W on the polythene bags then why there is no ban on the use of such bags?

Ans: Ordinary polythene bags are banned because they are non-biodegradable and do not break down in the environment. Bags marked D2W are degradable bags: unlike ordinary polythene, they break down into simple substances after some time instead of remaining in the soil and water as permanent pollution. That is why there is no ban on the use of such bags. (Note: the chapter itself does not explain D2W; this answer is based on the chapter's definition of biodegradable materials, which become part of the soil after being broken down by a natural process.)

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Evaporation is the change of water into water vapours; wet clothes dry, water on the floor dries up, and when sweat dries we feel cold due to evaporation.
  • Condensation is the change of gas (vapours) into liquid; water drops appear on the outer surface of a glass containing cold water or a cold drink.
  • Rusting is the change on the surface of iron due to oxygen and water (Iron + Oxygen + Water = Rusting); a brown layer forms and rusting is a chemical change because a new material is formed and it cannot be reversed.
  • Burning of wood, paper or coal is a chemical change in which carbon dioxide is produced; mixing vinegar with baking soda also forms bubbles of carbon dioxide.
  • The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas; a solid melts into liquid, a liquid freezes into solid, a liquid becomes gas by boiling and evaporation, and a gas becomes liquid by condensation.
  • Formation of fertilizer from leaves is a chemical change because bacteria and fungi decompose the leaves into a new material and the leaves cannot be got back.
  • When vinegar and baking soda are mixed, carbon dioxide escapes as bubbles so the weight becomes less; when ice melts, the weight of the water stays the same because melting is only a physical change.

Solved Exercises

Q: Explain evaporation giving examples from everyday life.

Ans: The change of water into water vapours is called evaporation. Water is released into the surrounding air continuously as water vapours from all wet surfaces, and this process takes place continuously from the surfaces of canals, lakes, rivers and oceans. Examples from everyday life: wet clothes dry due to evaporation, water fallen on the floor dries up after some time, and when our sweat dries up we feel cold due to evaporation.

Q: Define condensation.

Ans: The change of gas (vapours) into liquid is called condensation. When water vapours present in air collide with a cold surface, the heat of these particles is released, and the vapours change into liquid and stick to the surface. For example, water drops appear on the external surface of a glass containing cold water or a cold drink.

Q: What is rusting and which type of change is this?

Ans: The change that occurs on the surface of iron due to the action of oxygen and water is called rusting (Iron + Oxygen + Water = Rusting). A brown layer forms on iron objects like gates, doors and windows. Rusting is a chemical change, because a new material (rust) with different properties is formed and the change cannot be reversed.

Q: Give an example of chemical change in which carbon dioxide is produced?

Ans: Burning of wood, paper or coal is a chemical change in which carbon dioxide gas is produced along with ash and heat. Another example is mixing vinegar with baking soda: bubbles of carbon dioxide gas are formed, as seen in the vinegar and baking soda activity.

Q: Explain the three states of matter and their interconversion.

Ans: The three physical states of matter are solid, liquid and gas, in which the arrangement of particles is different. In solids the particles vibrate at fixed positions and are close together, in liquids they are less close and can move, and in gases they are far apart and move fast. Matter changes from one state to another by heating or cooling: a solid changes into liquid by melting, a liquid changes into solid by freezing, a liquid changes into gas by boiling and evaporation, and a gas changes into liquid by condensation.

Q: Weigh one fourth of a glass of vinegar and tea spoon of baking soda. Then mix them together. As a result, bubbles will be formed. Weigh this compound again. Now its weight will become less than the previous one. How will you explain the loss of the weight?

Ans: When vinegar and baking soda are mixed, a chemical change takes place and a new material, carbon dioxide gas, is formed. This gas appears as bubbles and escapes into the air. The weight becomes less because the weight of the escaped carbon dioxide gas is no longer present in the mixture being weighed.

Q: On mixing vinegar and boiling water bubbles are produced. Out of the two one is chemical change and the other one is a physical change. Explain.

Ans: The bubbles formed in boiling water are a physical change: on heating, water only changes its state into vapours or gas, no new material is formed, and the vapours can be changed back into water by condensation. The bubbles formed on mixing vinegar with baking soda are a chemical change: a new gas, carbon dioxide, with different properties is produced, and this change cannot be reversed.

Q: A student weighs a piece of ice and then allows it to melt. In your opinion what will be the weight of water and why?

Ans: The weight of the water will be the same as the weight of the piece of ice. Melting is a physical change in which only the state of matter changes from solid to liquid by absorption of heat. No new material is formed and no material is added or lost, so the weight remains the same.

Key Points

  • Light travels in air along a straight line.
  • Luminous objects emit their own light; non-luminous objects like the Moon, a chair and a book page are seen only when light reflected from them reaches our eyes.
  • Natural sources of light are the Sun, stars, lightning and the firefly; a candle and an electric bulb are artificial (man-made) sources.

Key Points

  • Transparent objects are those through which light can pass completely and we can see clearly across them, for example glass (window pane), clean water and a clear plastic sheet.
  • Our shadow is shortest at noon when the Sun is highest and almost overhead, and longest in the early morning and evening when the Sun is low near the horizon.

  • The intensity of sound decreases as the distance from its source increases, so a train moving away from us sounds fainter and fainter.
  • Hares and rats raise their ears when they hear a sound or feel danger, to catch the sound more clearly and find its direction so they can protect themselves in time.
  • Wood and charcoal are naturally non-luminous, but they can be made luminous by burning them, when they glow and emit light and heat.
  • Light travels much faster than sound: light travels 300,000 km in one second while sound travels only 340 metres per second in air, so we see lightning before we hear thunder.

Q: What is a transparent object? Write the name of three transparent objects.

Ans: The objects through which light can pass completely are called transparent objects. We can see clearly across them. Three transparent objects are: glass (window pane), clean water and clear plastic sheet (also glasses and magnifying glass).

Q: When is your shadow the shortest and the longest in the sunlight.

Ans: Our shadow is the shortest at noon, when the Sun is highest in the sky and almost overhead. It is the longest in the early morning and in the evening, when the Sun is low near the horizon. This is because the size and length of a shadow depend on the position of the light source relative to the object.

Q: The Moon is non-luminous like our Earth. How does it look luminous to us?

Ans: The Moon is a non-luminous object and does not emit its own light. Sunlight falls on the Moon and is reflected from its surface towards the Earth. This reflected light enters our eyes, so the Moon looks luminous (bright) to us.

Q: Can you be the winner while running with your shadow? Give the reason also.

Ans: No, we can never be the winner while running with our shadow. The shadow is formed by our own body blocking the sunlight, so it is always attached to us and moves with us at the same speed. It stays with us wherever we go, so we cannot leave it behind or run ahead of it.

Q: When a train is moving away from you, will the intensity of its sound increase or decrease?

Ans: The intensity of its sound will decrease. The intensity of sound depends on its loudness and decreases with the increase of distance from its source. As the train moves away, the distance increases, so its sound becomes fainter and fainter.

Ans: The ears of animals like the hare and the rat are actually raised up when they hear a sound or feel any danger around them. They raise their ears to catch the sound more clearly and to find out from which direction the sound is coming, so that they can protect themselves in time.

Ans: Yes, wood and charcoal can be made luminous by burning them. Wood and charcoal do not emit light in their natural state, but when they burn, they glow and emit light and heat, like a burning candle or lamp. So while burning, they behave as luminous objects.

Q: Have you seen the ears of a frog, locust and fish? How do these animals hear sounds?

Ans: These animals do not have outer ears like human beings, but they can still hear sounds. A frog hears through a round eardrum (tympanum) present on each side of its head behind the eye. A locust hears through an eardrum present on its body (abdomen). A fish hears through inner ears inside its head and feels the vibrations of sound passing through water with its body. In all of them, sound vibrations are received and sent to the brain. (Note: this Investigate question is not explained in the chapter text; it requires observation/research.)

Point to Ponder!

Q: The moon is not a natural source of light. Why it looks bright?

Ans: The moon is not a natural source of light because it does not emit its own light. It looks bright because sunlight falls on the moon and is reflected from its surface towards our eyes. Non-luminous objects like the moon are seen when light striking them is reflected towards our eyes.

Point to Ponder!

Q: The light from the Sun reaches us after passing through air atmosphere. Is air transparent or translucent?

Ans: Air is transparent. Sunlight reaches us after passing completely through the air, and we can see objects clearly across air, which shows that light passes completely through it.

Point to Ponder!

Q: What is the shape of shadow of a rotating object?

Ans: The shadow takes the shape of the object that blocks the light. As the object rotates, the part blocking the light keeps changing, so the shape of its shadow also keeps changing with the rotation.

Q: How is the shadow of a transparent object?

Ans: A transparent object does not form a shadow, because light passes completely through it and it does not block the path of light. A shadow is formed only when an opaque (non-transparent) object blocks the light.

Q: How is the shadow of a translucent object?

Ans: A translucent object forms a faint and light shadow, because it allows light to pass only partially and blocks only a part of the light.

Point to Ponder!

Q: When you see the Sun setting, is it really present on the horizon?

Ans: We see the setting Sun at the horizon because its light travels in a straight line through the air and reaches our eyes. The Sun is not actually present on the horizon; it only appears to be there as it goes down.

Q: Why do we see the image of a nearby tree or building in a lake?

Ans: The smooth surface of the lake water reflects light like a shining surface. More light is reflected from a smooth shining surface than from a dull surface, so the light coming from the tree or building is reflected by the water into our eyes and we see its image in the lake.

Q: The light is not reflected by a dark surface. How can we read the dark print on a book?

Ans: The white page reflects light towards our eyes, while the dark print reflects very little light. Because of this difference between the bright page and the dark letters, the letters become clear to our eyes and we can read the dark print on a book.

Point to Ponder!

Q: When we speak which thing does vibrate in our throat?

Ans: When we speak, the vocal cords in our throat vibrate. Sound is produced by a vibrating body, and the vibration of the vocal cords produces our voice.

Q: What vibrates in the given musical instruments? (Guitar, Drum, Flute)

Ans: In the guitar, the strings vibrate to produce sound. In the drum, the stretched skin (membrane) on its top vibrates when it is beaten. In the flute, the air inside the pipe vibrates to produce sound. In every case, sound is produced by a vibrating body.

Point to Ponder!

Q: Explosions are occurring in the Sun? Why do we not hear their sounds on the Earth?

Ans: We do not hear the sounds of explosions in the Sun because there are no particles in space between the Sun and the Earth. Sound cannot pass through space; a material medium like air, water or a solid is necessary for the propagation of sound, and there is no such medium in space.

Quick Quiz

Q: You can produce sound by plucking a stretched metal string or blowing air through a pipe. What is common and what is the difference between the two actions?

Ans: The common thing is that in both actions sound is produced by vibrations: a vibrating object produces sound. The difference is that on plucking, the stretched metal string itself vibrates, while on blowing through a pipe, the air inside the pipe vibrates to produce the sound.

Quick Quiz

Q: Why do we like to live at calm and quiet places?

Ans: We like to live at calm and quiet places because harsh and irritant sounds (noise) disturb us. In a noisy environment we cannot hear and understand one another, our thinking process is disturbed, we cannot concentrate on any task or study properly, and we cannot relax or sleep well. Noise also causes fatigue, anxiety and headaches, so calm and quiet places keep us comfortable and healthy.

Q: What benefit we may get form the awareness campaign regarding harmful effects of noise pollution?

Ans: Through an awareness campaign people learn about the harmful effects of noise pollution and the ways to control it, such as restricting the use of horns, restricting unnecessary use of loudspeakers, using good quality silencers, and planting more trees. When people act on this awareness, noise pollution is reduced and human health is protected from the harmful effects of noise.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A switch controls the flow of current in an electric circuit.
  • Current passes easily through conductors such as a steel paper clip, but not through glass, plastic or wood.
  • Every magnet, even a ring-shaped magnet, has two poles.
  • A freely suspended bar magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction.
  • Like poles repel each other: a north pole repels a north pole.
  • Metals such as aluminium, steel and silver are conductors; glass, ceramic and dry paper are insulators.

Solved Exercises

Q: The flow of current in an electric circuit is controlled by:

Options: (a) bulb (b) copper wire (c) switch (d) rubber

Correct answer: switch

Q: Current can easily pass through:

Options: (a) steel paper clip (b) glass strip (c) plastic comb (d) wooden spoon

Correct answer: steel paper clip

Q: How many poles are there of a ring shaped magnet?

Options: (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4

Correct answer: 2

Q: A freely suspended bar magnet always stays along

Options: (a) east-west direction (b) north-south direction (c) any direction (d) keeps oscillating

Correct answer: north-south direction

Q: Which one is the true statement?

Options: (a) North pole attracts north pole (b) North pole repels north pole (c) South pole repels north pole (d) South pole attracts south pole

Correct answer: North pole repels north pole

mcqs.q: The flow of current in an electric circuit is controlled by:
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is the switch. A switch is turned ON or OFF to allow or stop the flow of current in the circuit, while the bulb only glows and the wire only carries the current.

mcqs.q: Current can easily pass through:
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is the steel paper clip. Steel is a metal and a conductor, so current passes through it easily, while glass, plastic and wood are insulators through which current cannot pass.

mcqs.q: How many poles are there of a ring shaped magnet?
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is 2. Every magnet always has two poles, a north pole and a south pole, whatever its shape, so a ring-shaped magnet also has two poles.

mcqs.q: A freely suspended bar magnet always stays along
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is the north-south direction. A bar magnet suspended freely so that it can rotate comes to rest pointing north-south, which is also how its poles can be identified.

mcqs.q: Which one is the true statement?
mcqs.why: The book's keyed answer is that the north pole repels the north pole. Like poles repel each other, so north repels north and south repels south, while unlike poles attract each other.

mcqs.q: Which of these materials is an insulator?
mcqs.why: The solved Quick Quiz lists dry paper with glass and ceramic as insulators, like wood, rubber and plastic, through which current cannot pass. Copper, aluminium and steel are metals and are conductors.

mcqs.why: In the solved investigation, iron filings collect in the largest amount at the two ends of the magnet and very few stick in the middle. So the magnetic force is strongest at the ends, which are the magnet's poles.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A bulb lights in a closed circuit because the complete path lets electric current flow through it.
  • To light a bulb you need a cell or battery, a switch and metal connecting wires, besides the bulb itself.
  • An iron nail stuck to a magnet becomes a temporary magnet itself and can attract another nail, forming a chain.
  • A magnetic compass needle rests in the north-south direction; turn the compass until N aligns with the needle's north pole to read all directions.
  • A balloon rubbed with a woollen cloth gets a negative charge and sticks to a wall because it is charged with static electricity.
  • Like poles facing each other repel, so an upper ring magnet can float in the air above a lower one.
  • A magnet bar can be identified because it repels a known magnet, while iron is only attracted and aluminium is not attracted at all.

Solved Exercises

Q: Why does a bulb light up in a closed circuit?

Ans: In a closed circuit the path is complete, so electric current flows from the cell or battery through the wires, switch and bulb. The bulb lights up because electric current passes through it; the glowing bulb shows that current is flowing.

Q: You are given a bulb. What other components are required to light it up?

Ans: Besides the bulb, a cell or battery (the source of electric current), a switch to control the flow of current, and metal connecting wires are required. The bulb, cell/battery and switch joined by wires make the electric circuit, and the bulb lights up when the switch is turned ON.

Q: Why an iron nail stuck to a magnet attracts another nail?

Ans: The iron nail stuck to the magnet becomes a magnet itself under the effect of the strong magnetic force of the magnet. Being a (temporary) magnet, it attracts another iron nail, and in this way a chain of nails can be formed.

Q: How are directions found using a magnetic compass?

Ans: Put the magnetic compass on a table or ground, away from any other magnet or iron object. Its needle stays along the north-south direction. Rotate the compass slowly until the north pole of the needle is aligned with the north direction (N) marked on the compass. In this position the compass correctly shows all four directions marked on it.

Q: A balloon is charged by rubbing it with a woolen cloth. Why does it stick to a wall when brought near it?

Ans: On rubbing, the balloon acquires a negative charge and the woolen cloth a positive charge, i.e. the balloon becomes charged with static electricity. A charged object attracts the wall when brought near it, so the charged balloon sticks to the wall.

Q: Two ring magnets are shown on a wooden stand. The upper magnet rises up and is suspended in air as shown in the figure. a. Why does the upper magnet float in the air?

Ans: The two ring magnets are placed with like poles facing each other. Two like magnetic poles repel each other, and this repulsion pushes the upper magnet up and balances its weight, so it stays suspended (floats) in the air above the lower magnet.

Q: Two ring magnets are shown on a wooden stand. The upper magnet rises up and is suspended in air as shown in the figure. b. Label the N and S-poles of the magnets.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Two flat ring magnets are threaded on a vertical rod fixed on a rectangular wooden base (the wooden stand). The lower ring magnet rests on the base and the upper ring magnet floats in air above it, with a gap between the two. The top face of the upper magnet is labelled N, so its lower, facing face is S. The upper, facing face of the lower magnet is also S and its bottom face (touching the base) is N. The facing S–S poles are like poles, and their repulsion keeps the upper magnet suspended.

Q: There is a bar magnet without any indication. How will you identify its south pole?

Ans: Suspend the bar magnet freely with a thread so that it can rotate. It will come to rest in the north-south direction. The end that points towards the south is its south pole and the end pointing towards the north is its north pole. It can also be checked with a magnet of known poles: the end attracted by the north pole of the known magnet is the south pole.

Q: There are three similar metal bars. One is a magnet, the second one is that of iron and third bar is of aluminium. How would you identify each bar?

Ans: Bring a known magnet near each bar one by one. The aluminium bar is not attracted at all, because aluminium is a non-magnetic material. Both the magnet bar and the iron bar are attracted, so test them against each other: the bar that also repels a pole of the known magnet (like poles repel) is the magnet, while the iron bar is only attracted and never repels — it is the iron bar.

Q: A plastic comb charged with a woolen cloth is touched with an iron key. What do you observe? Give an example of similar phenomenon in daily life.

Ans: The iron key is a conductor, so the charge on the comb flows through the key and the comb is discharged; a tiny spark may be seen (with a small crackling sound) and the comb no longer attracts paper bits. A similar phenomenon in daily life is lightning: clouds charged by rubbing with air produce a big spark when clouds having opposite charges come near each other, which is also a kind of static electricity.

lessons.title: Investigate and Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Investigate and Project Work

Q: You are provided bar magnet, paper pins, glass, plastic, aluminium, steel plates and a wooden board. Investigate which material allows magnetic attraction to pass through it?

Ans: Place paper pins on one side of each plate/board and bring the bar magnet on the other side. The pins are attracted through the glass, plastic, aluminium and wooden board, because these are non-magnetic materials and allow magnetic attraction to pass through them. The attraction does not pass through the steel plate, because steel is a magnetic material and stops (absorbs) the attraction itself.

Q: You are provided with a water tub, cardboard, magnet, sellotape. Make a boat using the materials provided to you whose forward or backward motion can be controlled by another magnet.

Ans: Make a small boat from the cardboard and fix (tape) a magnet on it. Float the boat in the water tub. Bring another magnet near the boat without touching it: when the opposite pole faces the boat's magnet, the boat is attracted and moves forward towards it, and when the like pole faces it, the boat is repelled and moves backward. In this way the forward and backward motion of the boat is controlled by the second magnet.

Q: You are given a cardboard, torch bulb, electric cell, screws, and connecting wires. Design and make a test board for 4 science quizzes so that the bulb light up on the correct answer only.

Ans: On the cardboard, write 4 quiz questions with their answer choices, and fix a pair of screws (terminals) for each question–answer pair. Behind the board, connect wires so that only the screw of the correct answer completes the circuit between the electric cell and the torch bulb. When the free wire is touched to the screw of the correct answer, the circuit becomes closed, current flows and the bulb lights up; for a wrong answer the circuit stays open and the bulb does not light.

lessons.title: Points to Ponder, Quick Quizzes and Investigate
lessons.notes_html:
Points to Ponder, Quick Quizzes and Investigate

Point to Ponder!

Q: When a plastic comb is pulled through dry hair, it is negatively charged. What is the charge on the hair? What is the cause of hair to push apart?

Ans: The hair gets the opposite, positive charge, because on rubbing the comb and the hair acquire opposite charges. Each hair carries the same (positive) charge, and similar charges repel each other, so the hairs push apart and stand up.

Point to Ponder!

Q: If battery connections are reversed in a closed circuit, will the bulb glow?

Ans: Yes, the bulb will still glow. Reversing the battery only reverses the direction of flow of current; the circuit is still complete (closed), so current still passes through the bulb and it glows.

Quick Quiz

Q: Name any three conductors and insulators other than those mentioned here.

Ans: Conductors: aluminium, steel and silver — like iron and copper, these are metals and allow current to pass through them. Insulators: glass, ceramic and dry paper — like wood, rubber and plastic, current cannot pass through them.

Point to Ponder!

Q: You must have heard building set on fire by short circuit. How it can be avoided?

Ans: It can be avoided by using a fuse (or a circuit breaker) in the circuit. In a short circuit the current becomes excessive; the fuse wire melts and blows at once, the circuit breaks and the current stops flowing, so the wires and appliances do not catch fire.

Investigate:

Q: Find out which part of the magnet attracts strongly using a magnet and iron filling.

Ans: When a magnet is placed in iron filings, the filings collect in the largest amount at the two ends of the magnet and very few stick in the middle. So the magnet attracts most strongly at its ends, which are its magnetic poles; the magnetic force of the magnet is the strongest at the poles.

Point to Ponder!

Q: Can you make two magnets having one pole each by breaking a bar magnet?

Ans: No. When a bar magnet is broken, each piece becomes a complete magnet with its own north and south poles. A magnet always has two poles; a magnet with only one pole cannot be made.

Point to Ponder!

Q: How will you identify the north and south poles of an electromagnet? If battery terminals are reversed do the poles also change?

Ans: Bring a known bar magnet near each end of the electromagnet: the end that is repelled by the north pole of the bar magnet is the north pole of the electromagnet, and the end attracted by it is the south pole (a magnetic compass can be used in the same way). Yes, if the battery terminals are reversed, the direction of current in the coil reverses and the poles of the electromagnet also change — the north pole becomes the south pole and vice versa.

Quick Quiz

Q: Electric crane can lift iron objects from the scrap easily. How are they dropped in a truck to carry to a factory?

Ans: The crane uses an electromagnet. To drop the iron objects into the truck, the current in the electromagnet is switched OFF. The electromagnet is a temporary magnet and does not remain a magnet when the current is stopped, so the iron objects fall down into the truck.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The crust is the part of the Earth we live on, and its soil supports the growth of crops, vegetation and plants.
  • Clay soil is used for pottery: its particles are very small, it is soft, sticky and brownish, holds more water, can be moulded, and hardens when dried.
  • Humus is obtained from decayed plants and insects; it retains moisture in the soil and makes the soil fertile.
  • About 70% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, about 97% of that water is salty ocean water, and fresh water is only about 1%, so sea water cannot be drunk.
  • Water is found as a solid in ice and glaciers, as a liquid in oceans, rivers, lakes, springs, rain and underground water, and as a gas in water vapours in the air.
  • Silt (fertile soil) is about 45% sand and other minerals, about 25% air, about 25% water and about 5% humus.
  • Clay soil is used to plaster village houses because wet clay is soft and sticky, can be spread and moulded, and dries hard while keeping its shape.

Solved Exercises

Q: Name the outer layer of the Earth? What is its importance in our life?

Ans: The outer layer of the Earth is called the crust. It is the part of the Earth on which we live; it contains lofty mountains, deep oceans, rivers, deserts, green fields and rural and urban dwellings, and its soil supports the growth of crops, vegetation and plants, which are essential for life on Earth.

Q: Which soil is useful to make pottery? What are its properties?

Ans: Clay soil is useful to make pottery. Its particles are very small in size; the soil is soft, sticky and brownish in colour and can hold more water. Wet clay can be moulded into any shape, it retains its shape when dried and becomes more hard; dry clay is very hard.

Q: Which matter is obtained from the decayed plants and insects?

Ans: Humus is obtained from the decayed plants and insects (dead animal and plant matter). Humus is the organic matter produced by the decay of vegetables, plants and dead animal matter; it retains moisture in the soil and makes the soil fertile.

Q: How much part of the Earth's surface consists of oceans? Why we cannot drink sea water?

Ans: About 70% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, and about 97% of this water is the salted water in the oceans. We cannot drink sea water because it is salted (salty), and salty ocean water is not drinkable; the fresh water available to mankind is only about one percent.

Q: Where the water is found in the form of solid, liquid and gas (vapours)?

Ans: In solid form water is found as ice and glaciers (about 2% of water is frozen in the form of glaciers). In liquid form it is found in oceans, rivers, lakes, springs, rain and underground water. In gas form it is found as water vapours in the air, formed when the warmth of the Sun evaporates water from water bodies to form clouds.

Q: Label the diagram of the water cycle.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The diagram shows a water body (sea/lake) on the right with green land and mountains on the left, the Sun shining above and clouds in the sky. The four labels are: Evaporation — the box on the right, where wavy arrows rise from the water and land, showing water changing into vapours by the warmth of the Sun; Condensation — the box at the top near the Sun and clouds, where the vapours cool and form clouds; Precipitation — the box on the left over the mountain, where the clouds release water as rain (or snow) falling on the mountains and land; Collection — the box at the bottom over the water body, where the rain water collects through lakes, streams and rivers into the sea, and some is absorbed by land to become underground water. The cycle then repeats.

Q: Which soil is used to plaster the houses in village? Which property of the soil is useful to do so?

Ans: Clay soil is used to plaster the houses in villages. The useful property is that clay is soft and sticky when wet, can be spread and moulded into any shape, holds more water, and when it dries it retains its shape and becomes very hard, giving the walls a smooth, hard plaster.

Q: How do the plant roots and other creatures inside the Earth respire?

Ans: Plant roots and other creatures inside the Earth respire through the air present in the soil. Soil contains water and air which are essential for life, and this air in the spaces of the soil is used by roots and the living things in the soil for breathing.

Investigate and Project Work

Q: You have heard the devastation of floods. What is its reason? How the surplus water of floods can be made useful?

Ans: Floods are caused when rivers receive far more water than usual — from heavy rains and the melting of ice and glaciers — and the extra water overflows from rivers onto the surrounding land, causing devastation. The surplus flood water can be made useful by storing it, for example in dams, lakes and reservoirs, and by letting it soak into the ground to increase underground water, so that it can later be used for drinking, washing and irrigation instead of being wasted.

Q: Find out from the plant nursery or a gardener which soil is useful for growing plants? Prepare such soil in pots in your home or school. Grow plants by putting seeds in that soil.

Ans: The gardener/nursery shows that silt (fertile soil) is useful for growing plants, because it is a mixture of sand, clay and humus, holds more water than sandy soil and provides water and minerals to plants. Prepare such soil in pots at home or school, put seeds in that soil, water it, and the plants will grow in it.

Q: Collect samples of sand, clay and silt from various places. Mix a little water in each sample. Which soil can be shaped into a lump? Make simple toys or pots from this soil. Dry them in the sun. Colour their surfaces and place them on the shelf in the classroom.

Ans: Only clay soil can be shaped into a lump, because wet clay is soft and sticky and can be moulded into any shape, and it retains its shape when dried and becomes more hard; sand and silt do not hold a shape in this way. So make simple toys or pots from wet clay, dry them in the sun, colour their surfaces and place them on the shelf in the classroom.

Quick Quizzes and Points to Ponder

Quick Quiz

Q: A peach is cut into half. Label its parts showing resemblance with the structure of the Earth. Match the resemblance of its peel, pulp and seed with the parts of the Earth.

Ans: Diagram (in words): A peach cut into half shows three parts — a thin outer peel (skin), the thick soft fleshy pulp in the middle, and a hard seed in the centre. The peel resembles the crust, the outer thin layer of the Earth; the pulp resembles the mantle, the biggest middle layer under the crust; and the seed resembles the core, the central part of the Earth.
